implementation_notes: TypeScript cannot overload operators, so the instance is an object literal typed as a Monoid<T> with identity and combine, plus a generic fold. The types add value here: the law test is a plain type-level statement (combine: (a: T, b: T) => T with identity: T) and a monoid can be constrained in a generic function's type parameter so a caller cannot supply something that does not satisfy the interface. Array.concat and Array.reduce are the built-ins; reduce's initial value argument is required by the type signature, which is a nice safety property JavaScript itself does not give you.
idiom_name: Monoid<T> = { identity: T; combine(a: T, b: T): T } with a generic fold and a type constraint
pitfalls: Array.concat copies the left operand, so a fold over many arrays is quadratic; flatten once instead.
ts.reduce without an initial value throws on an empty array and the type signature will not stop you - always pass m.identity.
number addition is not associative in IEEE 754, so a parallel reduce over doubles can differ from the sequential result; the Monoid interface cannot express the caveat.
Typing identity as T rather than a literal type means a wrong identity is not caught; a satisfies-checked literal type is stricter where it matters.
